## From familiar models to stLMM

Small-area estimation combines information across areas when individual area
samples are sparse. These examples use datasets from `sae` and `survey` to show
how familiar models translate into `stLMM` [@MolinaMarhuenda2015sae;
@Lumley2004survey]. Milk expenditure and poverty use **area-level** responses:
direct estimates with supplied sampling variances. Corn production and school
achievement use **unit-level** responses, followed by population prediction.

The `sae` comparisons fit the same Gaussian response and random-effect models
by REML and report empirical best linear unbiased predictors (EBLUPs).
`stLMM` averages over posterior parameter uncertainty under explicit priors.
Point estimates can be close without uncertainty measures being identical:
posterior credible intervals and frequentist mean squared errors (MSEs) have
different interpretations. `survey` handles sampling weights and design-based
estimation; an IID effect in `stLMM` does not substitute for a survey design.

```{r packages}
library(stLMM)
library(sae)
library(survey)
library(ggplot2)

n_samples <- 12000L
burn <- 2000L
keep <- list(start = burn + 1L, thin = 10L)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
```

All fits use three chains and explicitly select `collapse_iid = TRUE`.
For these Gaussian models, `recover()` draws the IID effects after fitting.
We recover every tenth post-burn iteration to limit prediction storage.
The default separate IID
strategy is described in the
[grouped-effects article](a14-lme4-validation.html#iid-sampling-strategies).
Fixed coefficients have the default flat prior. The half-$t$ priors below
are on standard deviations in the supplied response units; covariates are not
automatically scaled. The models assume independent area effects and residual
errors, with the two collections also independent of one another.

```{r display-helpers}
#| code-summary: "Show plotting and summary helpers"
prediction_draws <- function(x) as.matrix(as_samples(x, metadata = FALSE))
area_intervals <- function(x){
  data.frame(mean = colMeans(x), lower = apply(x, 2, quantile, 0.025),
             upper = apply(x, 2, quantile, 0.975))
}
compare_areas <- function(tab, unit, mse = NULL){
  p <- ggplot(tab, aes(reference, mean)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey45")
  if(!is.null(mse)){
    tab$reference_lower <- tab$reference - qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(mse)
    tab$reference_upper <- tab$reference + qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(mse)
    p <- p + geom_errorbar(data = tab,
      aes(xmin = reference_lower, xmax = reference_upper),
      orientation = "y", width = 0, color = "grey55", alpha = 0.5)
  }
  limits <- range(tab$reference, tab$mean, tab$lower, tab$upper,
                  tab$reference_lower, tab$reference_upper)
  p +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0,
                  color = stlmm_color("primary"), alpha = 0.45) +
    geom_point(color = stlmm_color("primary"), size = 1.6) +
    coord_equal(xlim = limits, ylim = limits) +
    labs(x = paste0("sae EBLUP (", unit, ")"),
         y = paste0("stLMM posterior mean (", unit, ")"))
}
parameter_comparison <- function(fit, reference, example){
  p <- summary(fit, parameters = names(reference), burn = burn)$parameters
  labels <- names(reference)
  labels[labels == "iid_1_sigma_sq"] <- "Area variance"
  labels[labels == "tau_sq"] <- "Residual variance"
  data.frame(Example = example, Parameter = labels,
    stLMM = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", p[, "mean"],
                    p[, "q2.5"], p[, "q97.5"]),
    REML = round(unname(reference), 3))
}
```

## Milk expenditure: an area-level model

The `sae::milk` data contain 43 direct estimates of mean expenditure, their
standard errors, and a four-level major-area classification. Following the
[`sae` Fay–Herriot example](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/sae/sae.pdf),
write

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\theta_d &= \theta_d + e_d,\qquad
\theta_d = \beta_0 + \mathbf{x}_d^\top\mathbf{\beta} + u_d,\\
u_d&\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2),\qquad e_d\sim N(0,v_d).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\mathbf{x}_d$ contains major-area indicators and $v_d=\mathrm{SD}_d^2$
is treated as known. The independent $u_d$ allow each small area's mean to
depart from its major-area regression mean. Noisier direct estimates receive
more smoothing [@FayHerriot1979].

```{r milk-data}
data(milk, package = "sae")
milk$MajorArea <- factor(milk$MajorArea)
milk$SmallArea <- factor(milk$SmallArea)
milk$vhat <- milk$SD^2
milk_sae <- sae::mseFH(yi ~ MajorArea, vardir = vhat, data = milk)
```

```{r milk-fit}
#| code-fold: false
milk_fit <- stLMM(
  yi ~ MajorArea + iid(SmallArea) + resid(model = "fixed", variance = vhat),
  data = milk, priors = list(iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = half_t(3, 0.25))),
  collapse_iid = TRUE, n_samples = n_samples, chains = 3,
  chain_control = list(seed = 201), verbose = FALSE
)
set.seed(1201)
milk_rec <- recover(milk_fit, sub_sample = keep)
milk_draws <- prediction_draws(predict(milk_rec))
```

These are draws of the latent area means $\theta_d$. We leave `y_samples = FALSE`:
adding sampling-error draws would instead predict another direct survey estimate.

```{r milk-comparison, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=5}
milk_tab <- cbind(area_intervals(milk_draws), reference = milk_sae$est$eblup)
compare_areas(milk_tab, "expenditure units", mse = milk_sae$mse)
```

Each point is an area; vertical bars are central 95% posterior credible intervals.
Horizontal bars are approximate 95% frequentist intervals for the same area
means, calculated as EBLUP $\pm 1.96\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}}$ using
`mseFH()` [@MolinaMarhuenda2015sae]. Their coverage relies on a normal
approximation; they are not posterior probability statements. Both estimates
use the same data, so bar overlap is not a test of agreement.
All scatterplots use matching axis limits and equal units on both axes;
the 45-degree diagonal denotes equal point estimates. The mean absolute difference is
`r signif(mean(abs(milk_tab$mean - milk_tab$reference)), 3)` expenditure units.
The median posterior SD is `r round(median(apply(milk_draws, 2, sd)), 3)`,
while the median square root of the `sae` MSE is
`r round(median(sqrt(milk_sae$mse)), 3)`. Neither is a direct estimate's sampling SE.

## Spanish poverty: survey estimates into an area model

The [survey SAE vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/survey/vignettes/survey-sae.html)
uses synthetic income data for 52 Spanish provinces. Define poverty using its
threshold, 60% of the sample median income. With known province sizes $N_d$,
the weighted direct estimate is
$\widehat p_d=N_d^{-1}\sum_{i\in s_d}w_i\,\mathbf{1}(y_i<z)$.
The basic smoothing model is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat p_d &= p_d + e_d,\qquad p_d=\beta_0+u_d,\\
u_d&\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2),\qquad e_d\sim N(0,v_d).
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a Gaussian working model for a survey estimate, rather than a binomial
model for the individual records. Both smoothers receive exactly the same
direct estimates and variances. We use survey's with-replacement variance
approximation from the supplied weights; full sampling-design information is
not supplied with these synthetic records.

```{r poverty-data}
data(incomedata, package = "sae")
data(sizeprov, package = "sae")
incomedata$poor <- as.integer(incomedata$income < 0.6 * median(incomedata$income))
income_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~weight, data = incomedata)
direct <- svyby(~poor, ~provlab, income_design, svytotal)
N <- sizeprov$Nd[match(direct$provlab, sizeprov$provlab)]
poverty <- data.frame(provlab = direct$provlab,
  estimate = coef(direct) / N, vhat = SE(direct)^2 / N^2)
poverty_sae <- sae::mseFH(estimate ~ 1, vardir = vhat, data = poverty)
```

```{r poverty-fit}
#| code-fold: false
poverty_fit <- stLMM(
  estimate ~ 1 + iid(provlab) + resid(model = "fixed", variance = vhat),
  data = poverty, priors = list(iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = half_t(3, 0.1))),
  collapse_iid = TRUE, n_samples = n_samples, chains = 3,
  chain_control = list(seed = 202), verbose = FALSE
)
set.seed(1202)
poverty_rec <- recover(poverty_fit, sub_sample = keep)
poverty_draws <- prediction_draws(predict(poverty_rec))
```

```{r poverty-comparison, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=5}
poverty_tab <- cbind(area_intervals(poverty_draws), reference = poverty_sae$est$eblup)
compare_areas(100 * poverty_tab, "percent", mse = 100^2 * poverty_sae$mse)
```

Horizontal and vertical bars follow the milk comparison's conventions.
The mean absolute difference is
`r signif(100 * mean(abs(poverty_tab$mean - poverty_tab$reference)), 3)` percentage
points. The Gaussian model does not constrain probabilities to $[0,1]$; its
central intervals here lie within that range. Near the boundaries, a suitable
transformation and transformed sampling variances would need consideration.

`survey::svysmoothArea()` also offers Bayesian smoothing through SUMMER/INLA,
with PC priors. Here we use `survey` for direct estimation and `sae` for the
REML reference; this is not an INLA–MCMC comparison under matching priors.
The supplied sampling variances are treated as fixed in both fits.

## Iowa corn: a unit-level model and a population mean

The `cornsoybean` data contain 37 sampled land segments in 12 counties. The
companion data supply county sizes and population means of satellite pixel
counts. We reproduce the corn model used by `sae::eblupBHF()`:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{di}&=\beta_0+\beta_c\,\mathrm{CornPix}_{di}
+\beta_s\,\mathrm{SoyBeansPix}_{di}+u_d+\epsilon_{di},\\
u_d&\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2),\qquad\epsilon_{di}\sim N(0,\tau^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

The response is corn hectares per segment. A county intercept is shared by
its segments; residual errors are independent across segments. This BHF
model assumes sampling is ignorable conditional on the modeled information
[@BatteseHarterFuller1988]. Corn and soybean pixel counts are predictors of
one response, so this is a univariate model.

```{r corn-data}
data(cornsoybean, package = "sae")
data(cornsoybeanmeans, package = "sae")
cornsoybean$County <- factor(cornsoybean$County)
corn_sae <- sae::eblupBHF(CornHec ~ CornPix + SoyBeansPix, dom = County,
  meanxpop = cornsoybeanmeans[, c("CountyIndex", "MeanCornPixPerSeg", "MeanSoyBeansPixPerSeg")],
  popnsize = cornsoybeanmeans[, c("CountyIndex", "PopnSegments")], data = cornsoybean)
```

```{r corn-fit}
#| code-fold: false
corn_fit <- stLMM(
  CornHec ~ CornPix + SoyBeansPix + iid(County), data = cornsoybean,
  priors = list(iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = half_t(3, 50)), tau_sq = half_t(3, 50)),
  collapse_iid = TRUE, n_samples = n_samples, chains = 3,
  chain_control = list(seed = 203), verbose = FALSE
)
set.seed(1203)
corn_rec <- recover(corn_fit, sub_sample = keep)
```

The target is the finite-population county mean:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar Y_d&=\frac{\sum_{i\in s_d}y_{di}+(N_d-n_d)\bar Y_{d,r}}{N_d},\\
\bar Y_{d,r}\mid\mathbf{\beta},u_d,\tau^2&\sim
N\!\left(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{d,r}^{\top}\mathbf{\beta}+u_d,
\frac{\tau^2}{N_d-n_d}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Observed responses stay fixed. Population covariate means and sample sums
give the nonsampled covariate means. We predict those means and add the
appropriate residual uncertainty; no individual nonsampled records are needed.

```{r corn-population}
#| code-summary: "Show finite-population prediction"
sums <- aggregate(cbind(CornHec, CornPix, SoyBeansPix) ~ County, cornsoybean, sum)
sums <- sums[match(cornsoybeanmeans$CountyIndex, sums$County), ]
N <- cornsoybeanmeans$PopnSegments
n <- cornsoybeanmeans$SampSegments
nonsample <- data.frame(County = cornsoybeanmeans$CountyIndex,
  CornPix = (N * cornsoybeanmeans$MeanCornPixPerSeg - sums$CornPix) / (N - n),
  SoyBeansPix = (N * cornsoybeanmeans$MeanSoyBeansPixPerSeg - sums$SoyBeansPix) / (N - n))
mu <- prediction_draws(predict(corn_rec, newdata = nonsample))
tau_sq <- as_samples(corn_fit, burn = burn, thin = keep$thin)$tau_sq
set.seed(2203)
noise <- matrix(rnorm(length(mu)), nrow(mu)) * sqrt(tau_sq)
corn_draws <- sweep(mu, 2, N - n, "*") + sweep(noise, 2, sqrt(N - n), "*")
corn_draws <- sweep(sweep(corn_draws, 2, sums$CornHec, "+"), 2, N, "/")
```

The residual variances come from the original fit on the iteration grid used
by `recover()`, preserving their pairing with the predicted county means.

```{r corn-comparison, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=5}
corn_tab <- cbind(area_intervals(corn_draws), reference = corn_sae$eblup$eblup)
compare_areas(corn_tab, "hectares per segment")
```

The mean absolute difference is
`r round(mean(abs(corn_tab$mean - corn_tab$reference)), 2)` hectares per segment.
Only posterior intervals are shown: `eblupBHF()` returns point estimates;
EBLUP MSE estimation would require a separate calculation, such as `pbmseBHF()`.
With only 12 counties, uncertainty about the county variance remains substantial;
close county estimates do not imply equally precise variance estimates.

## California schools: sampled and unsampled counties

The [`survey` API data](https://r-survey.r-forge.r-project.org/pkgdown/docs/reference/api.html)
include a population of 6,194 schools and a 200-school sample stratified by
school type. We extend that example to county means, using the previous
year's score as auxiliary information:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{API00}_{di}&=\beta_0+\beta_a\,\mathrm{API99}_{di}
+\mathbf{x}_{di}^{\top}\mathbf{\beta}_t+u_d+\epsilon_{di},\\
u_d&\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2),\qquad\epsilon_{di}\sim N(0,\tau^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

The indicators $\mathbf{x}_{di}$ represent school type, the sampling strata.
The outcome model treats selection as ignorable conditional on these covariates.
The design-based comparison uses supplied weights, strata, and finite-population
corrections. Both target a mean across schools, not a student-weighted mean.

```{r school-data}
data(api, package = "survey")
school_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw,
                           fpc = ~fpc, data = apistrat)
school_direct <- svyby(~api00, ~cnum, school_design, svymean)
```

```{r school-fit}
#| code-fold: false
school_fit <- stLMM(
  api00 ~ api99 + stype + iid(cnum), data = apistrat,
  priors = list(iid_1 = list(sigma_sq = half_t(3, 100)), tau_sq = half_t(3, 100)),
  collapse_iid = TRUE, n_samples = n_samples, chains = 3,
  chain_control = list(seed = 204), verbose = FALSE
)
set.seed(1204)
school_rec <- recover(school_fit, sub_sample = keep)
```

The sample represents 40 of the 57 counties. Prediction for the other 17
requires `allow_new_levels = TRUE`. Their county effects are drawn from the
posterior population distribution, including that uncertainty in predictions.
We use the observed-plus-nonsampled calculation above. Because the model is
Gaussian and linear, nonsampled schools can be summarized by county and
school type without changing the distribution of their total. API scores for
2000 outside the sample are used only to evaluate the result.

```{r school-population}
#| code-summary: "Show prediction and county aggregation"
nonsample <- apipop[!apipop$snum %in% apistrat$snum, c("cnum", "stype", "api99")]
nonsample$n <- 1
cells <- aggregate(cbind(api99, n) ~ cnum + stype, nonsample, sum)
cells$api99 <- cells$api99 / cells$n
pred <- predict(school_rec, newdata = cells, allow_new_levels = TRUE)
mu <- prediction_draws(pred)
tau_sq <- as_samples(school_fit, burn = burn, thin = keep$thin)$tau_sq
set.seed(2204)
noise <- matrix(rnorm(length(mu)), nrow(mu)) * sqrt(tau_sq)
cell_totals <- sweep(mu, 2, cells$n, "*") + sweep(noise, 2, sqrt(cells$n), "*")
county_totals <- t(rowsum(t(cell_totals), cells$cnum))
county <- colnames(county_totals)
observed <- tapply(apistrat$api00, apistrat$cnum, sum)[county]
observed[is.na(observed)] <- 0
N <- as.numeric(table(apipop$cnum)[county])
school_draws <- sweep(sweep(county_totals, 2, observed, "+"), 2, N, "/")
```

Both estimators below are compared with known population means. Survey direct
estimates exist only for sampled counties. These are different methods:
stLMM additionally uses previous-year scores and pooling across counties.

```{r school-comparison, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
school_tab <- cbind(area_intervals(school_draws),
  truth = tapply(apipop$api00, apipop$cnum, mean)[county],
  direct = coef(school_direct)[match(county, school_direct$cnum)])
school_tab$sample <- ifelse(county %in% apistrat$cnum, "Sampled counties", "Unsampled counties")
limits <- range(school_tab[, c("truth", "mean", "direct", "lower", "upper")], na.rm = TRUE)
ggplot(school_tab, aes(truth)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey45") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0,
                color = stlmm_color("primary"), alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mean, color = "stLMM"), size = 1.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = direct, color = "Survey direct"), shape = 4, size = 1.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ sample) +
  coord_equal(xlim = limits, ylim = limits) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(stLMM = stlmm_color("primary"),
                                "Survey direct" = stlmm_color("secondary"))) +
  labs(x = "Known population county mean", y = "Estimated county mean", color = "Estimate") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r school-error}
sampled <- school_tab$sample == "Sampled counties"
rmse <- function(estimate, truth) sqrt(mean((estimate - truth)^2))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Counties = c("Sampled (40)", "Sampled (40)", "Unsampled (17)"),
  Estimate = c("Survey direct", "stLMM", "stLMM"),
  RMSE = round(c(rmse(school_tab$direct[sampled], school_tab$truth[sampled]),
                 rmse(school_tab$mean[sampled], school_tab$truth[sampled]),
                 rmse(school_tab$mean[!sampled], school_tab$truth[!sampled])), 2)
), caption = "County-mean errors for this sample, in API score points", row.names = FALSE)
```

These errors describe this particular sample. Repeated sampling would be needed
to assess design-based bias or interval coverage. The population outcomes are
known here; the latent means in the other examples are not known truths.

## Checking the comparison

The first three examples compare the same models and area targets under REML
and Bayesian estimation. The fourth shows a model-based extension of a survey
example. Check the target, supplied variances, and priors before
interpreting agreement. A close scatterplot alone does not validate an estimator
for other data or designs.

<details>
<summary>Regression coefficients and variance components</summary>

Posterior means and central 95% credible intervals are shown beside REML estimates.
The small number of Iowa counties makes its variance comparison less precise
than its area-mean comparison. Variance parameters below are on the variance
scale, even though their priors were specified on standard deviations.

```{r parameter-table}
milk_reference <- c(setNames(milk_sae$est$fit$estcoef$beta,
                             c("(Intercept)", "MajorArea2", "MajorArea3", "MajorArea4")),
                     iid_1_sigma_sq = milk_sae$est$fit$refvar)
poverty_reference <- c("(Intercept)" = poverty_sae$est$fit$estcoef$beta,
                        iid_1_sigma_sq = poverty_sae$est$fit$refvar)
corn_reference <- c(setNames(corn_sae$fit$fixed, c("(Intercept)", "CornPix", "SoyBeansPix")),
                     tau_sq = corn_sae$fit$errorvar, iid_1_sigma_sq = corn_sae$fit$refvar)
knitr::kable(rbind(parameter_comparison(milk_fit, milk_reference, "Milk"),
                   parameter_comparison(poverty_fit, poverty_reference, "Poverty"),
                   parameter_comparison(corn_fit, corn_reference, "Corn")), row.names = FALSE)
```

</details>
